title: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
network: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
cover_up: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.
what: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.

title: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
network: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
cover_up: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.
what: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.

title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.
what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

title: Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished
who: Gynaecologist Eduardo Vela
network: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
what: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987. It was the first trial in Spain over the 'stolen babies' of the Franco era and after. A judge had recorded about 30,000 cases of Spanish children taken, according to the report.

title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

title: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cover_up: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).
what: The Commission of Investigation's final report, published on 12 January 2021, covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 56,000 women and 57,000 children were placed or born in them between 1922 and 1998. About 9,000 children died there, about 15% of all the children in the institutions, with infant mortality about double the national average. The homes doubled as orphanages and adoption agencies, and women faced pressure to place their children for adoption; Ireland did not legislate for adoption until 1952. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for 'the profound generational wrong visited upon Irish mothers and their children'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)

title: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013
who: Australian governments, hospitals, churches and adoption agencies
what: From the late 1950s to the 1970s tens of thousands of babies of unmarried, mostly teenage mothers were taken for adoption, often without informed consent. A Senate Community Affairs References Committee report in February 2012 ('Commonwealth Contribution to Former Forced Adoption Policies and Practices') urged a national apology. Prime Minister Julia Gillard delivered it on 21 March 2013. Several state and territory parliaments had apologised before this, starting with Western Australia in 2010.

title: Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008)
who: Australian federal, state and territory governments; church and state missions and institutions
what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly removed from their families under government policies roughly between 1910 and 1970 and placed in institutions, missions, foster or adoptive families. The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 1997 report 'Bringing Them Home' estimated that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children were forcibly removed in that period, and recommended a national apology; Prime Minister John Howard refused, and Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised on 13 February 2008. Redress schemes followed, including Tasmania (2006) and NSW (2017), and in August 2021 a A$378 million Commonwealth scheme paying A$75,000 to each eligible survivor removed in the Northern Territory, the ACT or the Jervis Bay Territory (about 3,600 people).

title: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement
who: Federal government of Canada and provincial child welfare authorities
what: From the 1950s into the 1980s thousands of Indigenous children were taken from their families by child welfare authorities and placed with non-Indigenous foster and adoptive families. On 14 February 2017 Justice Edward Belobaba of the Ontario Superior Court (Brown v. Canada) ruled that Ottawa had failed in its duty of care to on-reserve children in Ontario removed between 1965 and 1984, who lost their language, culture and identity; the class was expected to number about 16,000. On 6 October 2017 Crown-Indigenous Affairs Minister Carolyn Bennett announced an agreement in principle worth about C$800 million: C$750 million for First Nations and Inuit people removed between 1951 and 1991 (C$25,000 each if there were more than 20,000 claimants, up to C$50,000 if fewer) and C$50 million for a reconciliation and healing foundation.

title: United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978
who: Bureau of Indian Affairs, US Children's Bureau, Child Welfare League of America
what: The Indian Adoption Project, administered by the Child Welfare League of America under a federal contract from the Bureau of Indian Affairs and the US Children's Bureau, placed 395 Native American children from 16 western states with white families between 1958 and 1967. In 1978 Congress passed the Indian Child Welfare Act, whose findings state that 'an alarmingly high percentage of Indian families are broken up by the removal, often unwarranted, of their children' by non-tribal agencies. In June 2001 CWLA executive director Shay Bilchik formally apologised, saying the project 'was wrong; it was hurtful; and it reflected a kind of bias that surfaces feelings of shame.'

title: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
who: Israeli state health and immigration institutions
what: More than 1,000 families, mostly immigrants from Yemen but also dozens from the Balkans, North Africa and other Middle Eastern countries, say babies taken to hospitals in Israel's early years disappeared after parents were told they had died; many believe they were given away for adoption. Three government inquiries since the 1960s concluded that most of the children died of disease and were buried without their parents being informed. In 2016 the government decided to put most of the inquiries' archives online. On 22 February 2021 the government expressed regret and approved a NIS 162 million compensation plan: NIS 150,000 for each child whose death was reported to the family at the time and NIS 200,000 for each child whose fate is unknown.

title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
network: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

title: France — Children of Creuse: 2,015 Réunionese children moved to mainland France
who: French state social services (DDASS); scheme led by Réunion MP Michel Debré
what: Between 1963 and 1982 the French state took roughly 2,000 children from Réunion who had been made wards of the state and sent them to depopulating rural departments of mainland France such as Creuse, promising their families a good education and a better future. Some were adopted; others stayed in homes or were made to work on farms. On 18 February 2014 the National Assembly passed a resolution stating that the state had failed in its moral responsibility towards these wards and that their right to maintain ties with their families had been insufficiently protected. No compensation payments have been planned.

title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.
what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.

title: Vietnam — Nam Dinh ring: 266 babies sold for foreign adoption
who: Heads of two provincial social welfare centres; doctors and nurses at village clinics
what: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.

title: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
what: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

title: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
who: Focus on Children, Utah agency run by Scott and Karen Banks
network: Focus on Children (Utah)
what: Samoan parents were told their children would go to the US temporarily for schooling, but the children were adopted permanently. A federal indictment on 28 February 2007 charged Scott and Karen Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. All pleaded guilty on 6 January 2009 to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; in February 2009 Judge David Sam sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.

title: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme
who: Paul Petersen, Maricopa County (Arizona) Assessor and adoption lawyer
what: Petersen, an elected Arizona official, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to the US, paying them about $10,000 to give up their babies and charging adoptive couples about $35,000, although the Compact of Free Association bars Marshallese travel to the US for adoption. Charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, he pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 (human smuggling, fraud, communication fraud) and was sentenced in December 2020 in federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison. He also fraudulently obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds for the women.

title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.
what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.

title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

title: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
what: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

title: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
what: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

title: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
what: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.

title: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
what: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.

title: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
what: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.

title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).
what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.

title: United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026)
who: Local authorities, religious organisations, NHS bodies, mother and baby homes
what: The Joint Committee on Human Rights report 'The Violation of Family Life: Adoption of Children of Unmarried Women 1949–1976' (15 July 2022) found many mothers did not want to give up their babies and were pressured by secrecy, shame and lack of support, and rejected the government's position that it was not responsible. The government declined to apologise in March 2023. On 2 July 2026 Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer gave a formal apology in the House of Commons, calling the practices 'embedded' across local authorities, religious organisations and parts of what is now the NHS, and announced a £4m support package (no compensation scheme).

title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

title: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens
who: Russian state
what: On 28 December 2012 President Putin signed a law banning the adoption of Russian children by US families, effective 1 January 2013. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler adopted by Americans who died in 2008 after being left for hours in a hot car; his adoptive father was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The law was widely seen as retaliation for the US Magnitsky Act, signed on 14 December 2012. In 2010 a US adoptive mother had sent her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a one-way flight back to Russia, causing outrage. (This is a closure event, not a trafficking finding.)

title: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
network: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho)
what: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.

title: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
what: In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that a $2 million special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States; Wikipedia, citing several sources, gives a total of over 3,300 children airlifted. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April 1975, killing many of the children on board (78, according to US Defense Intelligence Agency figures cited by Wikipedia). A lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans and had been given up under duress during wartime; poor families sometimes placed children in orphanages without intending to give them up, and many adoption records lacked parental consent.

title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
who: Salvadoran armed forces
cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.
what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.

title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

title: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
network: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
cover_up: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.
what: After the 1936–39 Civil War about 30,000 children were placed in state care under the Franco regime — mostly, in the words of a 2008 ruling by Judge Baltasar Garzón, 'war orphans with parents who were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding, or disappeared'. Children of single mothers held in homes run by the Patronato de Protección de la Mujer were also pressured into adoption. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from Spanish hospitals over five decades asked the attorney general to investigate an alleged network of doctors and nurses; lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies were taken. A 2026 study by forensic geneticists of Spain's National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences found no evidence of systematic hospital theft and called the 300,000 figure a hoax, while not denying the coercion in Francoist institutions or the 30,000 children placed in state care.

title: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
what: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.

title: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
network: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)
what: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).

title: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
network: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)
what: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.

title: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
what: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.

title: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
who: Baby 101 company
what: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

title: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
what: The Ideal Maternity Home in Nova Scotia, run by William and Lila Young from the late 1920s until 1947, promised discreet birthing and adoption for unmarried mothers. According to author Bette Cahill, people paid up to $10,000, usually disguised as a donation, to adopt babies from the home, while babies considered 'unmarketable' were fed only molasses and water; many died and were buried in butter boxes. Wikipedia, citing Cahill, adds that mothers were charged $500, that the provincial Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934, and that the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act; a 1946 Montreal Standard article described their 'baby farm rackets'.

title: Denmark — 1951 'little Danes' experiment: 22 Greenlandic children removed
who: Danish government, Danish Red Cross, Save the Children Denmark
what: In May 1951 Danish authorities, with Save the Children Denmark, had teachers and priests in Greenland identify children aged six to ten, and 22 Inuit children were sent to Danish foster families to be re-educated as 'little Danes'; many families were reluctant. About a year and a half later 16 returned to Greenland, where they were placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross and many never lived with their families again; six were adopted in Denmark. A 2020 report found half later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022, after legal action, the six survivors were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

title: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
who: French government and adoption associations
cover_up: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.
what: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.

title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.
what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.

title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

title: Switzerland — 'Kinder der Landstrasse': Yenish children removed by Pro Juventute (1926–1973)
who: Pro Juventute foundation, with federal and cantonal authorities
what: From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute foundation's 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse' (Charity for the Children of the Country Road) took around 600 Yenish children from their families and forcibly placed them in homes or foster families; around 2,000 children of the Swiss Traveller community are believed to have been affected by such measures overall. The persecution depended on authorities at every level of government, which were closely intertwined with Pro Juventute in personnel and co-funded the Hilfswerk. On 20 February 2025 the Swiss government, taking note of a legal opinion led by Professor Oliver Diggelmann, acknowledged that the persecution of Yenish and Sinti people was a crime against humanity under current international law (but not a 'cultural genocide'), and reaffirmed its apology. (Care agent covers Verdingkinder.)

title: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
what: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.

title: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
what: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

title: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
network: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
cover_up: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.
what: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.

title: Colombia — 1981 ring selling Andean children abroad with forged papers
who: Adoption trafficking ring
what: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. In 2003 Interpol issued a detention order for the manager of an uncertified Costa Rica-based adoption agency suspected of trafficking babies from Colombia in 2000–2002 (suspect, not convicted).

title: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
what: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.

title: United States — 'Baby Scoop Era' adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies (1945–1973)
who: Maternity homes, adoption agencies, social workers
what: From 1945 to 1973 up to 4 million US parents, mostly unmarried mothers, had children placed for adoption, often presented as the only option with little effort to help mothers keep their babies. Non-relative adoptions rose from about 33,800 in 1951 to 89,200 in 1970. No national official inquiry has been held (unlike Australia, Ireland and the UK).

title: Canada — maternity homes and post-war adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies
who: Maternity homes run mostly by the Catholic Church and the Salvation Army, some Anglican and United Church; Children's Aid Societies
what: Women sent to maternity homes for unwed mothers after the Second World War say they were coerced into giving up babies they wanted to keep through shaming, intimidation and withholding information about alternatives such as social assistance; one woman later found her file recorded that she had wanted to take her baby home. Origins Canada asked the churches to support a parliamentary or Senate inquiry (Anglican Journal, May 2014).

title: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
who: Online brokers; baby sellers
what: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.

title: United States / UK — 'internet twins' sold twice through an online adoption broker
who: Internet agency A Caring Heart (broker in California)
what: In 2000–01 a California-based internet adoption broker placed six-month-old twin girls first with a Californian couple, who paid about £4,000 and were then persuaded to return them to the birth mother, and then with a couple from north Wales who paid about £8,200 and adopted them in Arkansas. After the Welsh couple publicised the purchase in January 2001, Prime Minister Tony Blair promised action against trading children for adoption, Flintshire council took the twins into care under an emergency protection order, and on 9 April 2001 the High Court ruled they should be returned to the US. The FBI searched the broker's home near San Diego on 14 March 2001. The case led to UK adoption reform, including penalties for bringing children into the UK for adoption without approval.

title: North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'
who: Clwyd and Gwynedd county councils' children's homes, incl. Bryn Estyn; North Wales Police criticised
cover_up: The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.
what: Sir Ronald Waterhouse's tribunal took evidence from about 650 people who had been in care and published 'Lost in Care' in February 2000, finding widespread abuse over about 20 years in children's homes in North Wales. Allegations were reported across almost 40 homes, with the report concentrating on seven. Seven former care workers were convicted after a 1991 police inquiry, five of them from Bryn Estyn. The report found responses were 'too little and too late' and that children's interests were sacrificed to protect professional positions; officers of North Wales Police were among those accused.

title: Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings
who: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast Welfare Authority / Eastern Health and Social Services Board); RUC investigations; MI5
cover_up: Hart found MI5 'consistently obstructed a proper line of inquiry' during the 1980s RUC Caskey Phase Three investigation, and found numerous missed opportunities to detect and stop the abuse.
what: The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart reported on 20 January 2017. It confirmed that 38 boys at Kincora were sexually abused; three staff members, Joseph Mains, Raymond Semple and William McGrath, were convicted. Hart found that Kincora was not a homosexual brothel, that no security agency used it to entrap or blackmail men, and that there was 'no credible evidence' that prominent people such as civil servants, businessmen or Sir Maurice Oldfield were involved; he called the honey-trap claims 'unfounded myths'. He did criticise MI5 for obstructing the 1980s police investigation. Some former residents rejected the conclusions.

title: Northern Ireland Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (22 institutions, 1922–1995)
who: 22 children's homes and institutions run by the state, voluntary bodies and religious orders in Northern Ireland
what: The Hart Inquiry's 10-volume, roughly 2,300-page report, published 20 January 2017, examined abuse in 22 residential institutions in Northern Ireland between 1922 and 1995, reviewing hundreds of government and intelligence files. It found systemic failings and abuse including sexual abuse across state, voluntary and church-run homes and recommended redress and a public apology.

title: Jersey care system and Haut de la Garenne — Independent Jersey Care Inquiry
who: States of Jersey children's services; Haut de la Garenne children's home
cover_up: The inquiry found the authorities failed to build a culture of transparency, feeding perceptions of collusion and cover-up, and a 'small island culture' that was not countered.
what: The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry reported in July 2017 after hearing from about 450 people connected with Jersey's care system since 1945. It found the States of Jersey had been 'an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent', that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. Haut de la Garenne, centre of the 2007–2010 police investigation Operation Rectangle, was described as a symbol of the turmoil and the inquiry recommended its buildings be demolished. Chief Minister Ian Gorst apologised: 'We failed children who needed our care.'

title: Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA
who: London Borough of Lambeth; Shirley Oaks, South Vale and Angell Road children's homes
cover_up: Over 40 years only one senior employee was disciplined. The council did not tell a coroner that a boy found dead at Shirley Oaks in 1977 had alleged sexual abuse by his 'house father' Donald Hosegood; the inquiry asked the Metropolitan Police to consider a criminal investigation into this.
what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 27 July 2021 that children in Lambeth's care were subjected to decades of cruelty and sexual abuse from the 1960s. By June 2020 the council had complaints from 705 former residents; at Shirley Oaks, allegations were made against 177 staff or associated people involving at least 529 former residents. At Angell Road, children including some under five were systematically exposed to sexual abuse. The inquiry found racism, nepotism, corruption and mismanagement in the council, and that most children at Shirley Oaks (1980) and South Vale (1990–91) were Black.

title: Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA
who: Nottinghamshire County Council and Nottingham City Council residential and foster care; Beechwood Children's Home
cover_up: Only two disciplinary actions, both inadequate, followed the many allegations at Beechwood; known perpetrators were allowed to continue fostering and abused again.
what: IICSA reported on 31 July 2019 that sexual abuse was widespread in the two councils' residential and foster care in the 1970s–1990s. About 350 people reported abuse. From the late 1970s to 2019, 16 residential staff and 10 foster carers were convicted of sexually abusing children in their care, plus 12 convictions for harmful sexual behaviour by children against other children. The inquiry concluded that 'neither of the Councils learned from their mistakes'.

title: Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff
who: Medomsley Detention Centre for young offenders (Home Office Prison Service)
cover_up: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman (November 2025) found that knowledge of the abuse held by the Prison Service, police and Home Office was 'ignored and dismissed', families' complaints led to no action, and successive wardens were 'either complicit or incompetent'.
what: Medomsley held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, an officer who ran the kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and again in 2005 and died in 2010; the Ombudsman called him 'possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history'. Operation Seabrook (from 2013) identified 32 living suspects; five former officers were convicted in 2019 and another in 2023, eight former staff jailed in total. The Ombudsman's report of 12 November 2025, based on 8,000 documents and 74 witnesses, found the authorities failed in their duty to keep detainees safe.

title: Islington Council children's homes, London
who: London Borough of Islington children's homes and foster placements (42 homes)
cover_up: A 2018 report by Sarah Morgan QC found that councillor Sandy Marks knew of abuse allegations before the Evening Standard published them in 1992; the council leadership publicly denied the newspaper's reports at the time.
what: Survivors say children in Islington's 42 children's homes and in foster care were abused between the 1960s and 1990s; the Evening Standard exposed abuse in the homes in 1992. A 2018 independent report by Sarah Morgan QC into former councillor Sandy Marks found evidence linking her to the 'Fallen Angels' group (which she denies) but no evidence it affected her council duties or that she learned of organised abuse. Islington later set up a support payment scheme for survivors.

title: Kendall House girls' home, Gravesend — Proctor review
who: Kendall House, a Church of England children's home taking girls placed by social services
what: An independent review chaired by Dr Sue Proctor, commissioned by the Bishop of Rochester and published in July 2016, found that from 1967 girls as young as 11 were routinely given antidepressants, sedatives and antipsychotics, sometimes without medical assessment. Former residents were physically, emotionally and sometimes sexually abused, including two rapes while girls were held in isolation. The review heard from 20 former residents and examined records of 44. A 1980 television programme had already exposed the home.

title: Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's homes — Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry
who: Quarriers, Aberlour Child Care Trust and Barnardo's residential homes in Scotland
what: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's third case study findings, published 7 January 2020, concluded that children in residential care run by Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's between 1921 and 1991 suffered physical, emotional and sexual abuse. These voluntary providers cared for children placed by local authorities across Scotland.

title: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales)
who: Institutions across England and Wales: local authority care, churches, schools, custodial institutions, political parties, police
what: IICSA published its final report in October 2022 after 19 investigation reports, 325 days of public hearings, more than 700 live witnesses and almost 1,000 written statements, and over 200,000 documents. More than 6,200 victims and survivors took part in its Truth Project. It made 107 recommendations, including mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse. Its investigations found institutional failures by councils, police, churches and government departments.

title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
network: British child migration programmes
cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.
what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.

title: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers
who: Berlin Senate youth administration and state youth office (Landesjugendamt); sexologist Helmut Kentler (Pädagogisches Zentrum Berlin, later TU Hannover); network incl. Gerold Becker of the Odenwaldschule
network: Kentler network (West German youth welfare and pedagogy)
cover_up: University of Hildesheim researchers found the abuse was carried out and institutionalised under the responsibility of the Landesjugendamt and the Berlin Senate administration; Kentler died in 2008 without prosecution.
what: From the late 1960s (Kentler held a post at the Senate's Pädagogisches Zentrum from 1967 to 1976) West Berlin youth authorities, on the advice of Helmut Kentler, placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, as a form of 'resocialisation'. University of Hildesheim reports (2020 and final report 22 February 2024) reconstructed a nationwide network in science, youth welfare and administration that supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions and sexual violence, continuing beyond 2000. Some children were about five years old when placed. Berlin says known victims have received compensation.

title: Odenwaldschule, Heppenheim — abuse by headmaster Gerold Becker and teachers
who: Odenwaldschule (private, state-recognised progressive boarding school); headmaster Gerold Becker, music teacher Wolfgang Held
network: Kentler network (West German youth welfare and pedagogy)
cover_up: After victims came forward in 1998 and the Frankfurter Rundschau reported it in November 1999, a promised review did not take place; prosecutors in Darmstadt dropped the case under the statute of limitations. Becker died in 2010 without facing legal consequences.
what: Lawyers Claudia Burgsmüller and Brigitte Tilmann, a former judge, were called in by the school to investigate; their 2010 report identified more than a dozen perpetrators, with former headmaster Gerold Becker and a music teacher named as the main abusers from the late 1960s, and 17 witnesses testifying against Becker. Later counts put the victims at at least 132 pupils abused by teachers between the 1960s and 1990s; the victims' association says at least 20 teachers were responsible. The abuse, long covered up, became widely public in 2010; pupil numbers and funding fell and in April 2015 the school's sponsoring association announced its closure. Becker also appears in the Hildesheim research as a figure in the Kentler network.

title: Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender
who: Two men at a permanent campsite; youth welfare offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont; Lippe police
cover_up: Welfare authorities placed a foster girl with the main offender despite allegations about him. Police failed to act on repeated complaints, evidence disappeared from police archives, and a case worker manipulated and deleted files. The NRW parliamentary inquiry found 'authority failure' and said the men could have been stopped two years earlier.
what: On 5 September 2019 the Detmold regional court sentenced Andreas V. to 13 years and Mario S. to 12 years, both followed by preventive detention, for abusing 32 children at a campsite in Lügde from 1998 to 2018; police found 32,000 files of abuse material. Youth welfare authorities had placed a foster daughter with Andreas V. The North Rhine-Westphalia Landtag inquiry (interim report 24 March 2022) found failures by police and the youth offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont.

title: Round Table on Residential Care (Runder Tisch Heimerziehung) — West German children's homes 1950s–70s
who: State and church-run children's homes in West Germany
what: The Bundestag-appointed Round Table on residential care in the 1950s and 1960s presented its final report in December 2010. It found brutal discipline, humiliation, beatings and forced labour were common, and about one in three of those who contacted it reported sexual abuse. It recommended a fund of at least €120 million to be paid in equal thirds by the federal government, the states and the churches.

title: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
what: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.

title: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
what: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.

title: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
what: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

title: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
cover_up: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.
what: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.

title: Godhavn Report — Danish state children's homes 1945–1976
who: Danish state-run children's homes incl. Godhavn boys' home
what: The Godhavn Report, published 9 May 2011, examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976, finding neglect, physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22% of Godhavn residents had been given psychiatric drugs by psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld. No prosecutions followed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims in 2019.

title: Swedish inquiry into abuse in children's homes and foster care (Vanvårdsutredningen)
who: Swedish municipal children's homes and foster care
what: The government inquiry into abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980 reported in February 2011, recommending a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who suffered serious abuse; the apology ceremony was held at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up on 1 January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

title: Norwegian children's homes and special schools 1945–1980 (NOU 2004:23)
who: Norwegian municipal children's homes and state special schools
what: The official report NOU 2004:23 'Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen' found neglect and abuse, in part of a serious nature and including sexual abuse, in children's homes and special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities ran their own investigations and compensation schemes; in 2005 the Storting committee recommended adapting the state 'rettferdsvederlag' scheme with payments up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof.

title: Finland — maltreatment in child welfare substitute care 1937–1983
who: Finnish child welfare institutions and foster care
what: A Ministry of Social Affairs and Health study interviewed about 300 people who had been in child welfare substitute care between 1937 and 1983 and found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. The Finnish government made an official apology on 20 November 2016, Universal Children's Day.

title: France — children in state child welfare (ASE) exploited in prostitution
who: Aide sociale à l'enfance (departmental child welfare services)
what: A French parliamentary commission of inquiry report published in April 2025 estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services (ASE), which hold about 396,900 minors, are victims of prostitution. Lawyers asked the Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne departments for administrative reviews over children in care who were prostituted; teenagers are often housed in hotels with little supervision. A complaint was filed with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.

title: Notre-Dame de Bétharram school — National Assembly commission of inquiry
who: Notre-Dame de Bétharram, a Catholic private school under contract with the state; Ministry of Education inspection
cover_up: The commission wrote that 'in the absence of action from a minister who was informed and in a position to intervene', abuse continued for years; it found state inspection of private schools under contract was weak and sanctioned teachers could move between schools undetected.
what: Priests, teachers and staff are accused of sexual and physical abuse of pupils from 1957 to 2004, with about 200 complaints filed in 2025. The National Assembly commission of inquiry (rapporteurs Violette Spillebout and Paul Vannier) published its report on 2 July 2025 with 50 recommendations, including rebuilding state inspections. It did not directly implicate François Bayrou, who said he had not grasped the seriousness of information he received; Vannier separately accused him of misleading parliament.

title: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims
who: Government of Canada; schools operated by the Catholic, Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
network: Indian Residential School system (Canada)
cover_up: Under the settlement, claimants' IAP records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep or share them.
what: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher. By the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for injuries from physical and sexual abuse and 30,939 resolved. The Independent Assessment Process received 38,276 claims in total; adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants and the government compensated 4,415 more directly.

title: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
cover_up: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.
what: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.

title: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children — Restorative Inquiry
who: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children (provincially funded orphanage for Black children)
what: Former residents of the home, which operated from 1921, described neglect and emotional, physical and sexual abuse. A class action was settled and the provincial government apologised in 2014 to former residents and the African Nova Scotian community for harm caused by systemic racism. The Restorative Inquiry delivered its final report on 28 November 2019 in Halifax.

title: Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse
who: Cornwall Community Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police (Project Truth), local probation office, Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria-Cornwall
cover_up: Commissioner Glaude found the Diocese's $32,000 settlement with complainant David Silmser contained an illegal clause, and called Cornwall police's investigation of his complaint 'deeply flawed', though he found no conspiracy between police and diocese.
what: The Cornwall Public Inquiry under Commissioner G. Normand Glaude reported in December 2009 at a cost of over $50 million. It found systemic failures by police, probation and the Catholic diocese in responding to historical sexual abuse allegations against adults in positions of trust in Cornwall. On the long-rumoured paedophile 'clan', Glaude made no finding, saying no investigation had provided conclusive evidence.

title: Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario
who: Ontario provincial training school for girls (juvenile reformatory)
cover_up: Complaints of serious sexual abuse made by girls while at the school were reportedly ignored and never investigated.
what: Hundreds of women reported physical and sexual abuse while held as girls at the Grandview Training School, a government-run school for 'troubled' girls in Galt (now Cambridge), Ontario, which closed in 1976. Eight former staff members were charged and two were convicted. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite an investigation by Ontario Provincial Police and Waterloo Regional Police after the abuse became public in 1991, a survivors' group of more than 300 women seeking compensation, and a 1999 apology by MPP Jim Flaherty in the Ontario legislature on the province's behalf (these three points not re-confirmed in this pass).

title: Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation
who: US Department of the Interior / federal government; many schools run by churches with federal funding
network: Federal Indian boarding school system (US)
what: The Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative's Volume I (May 2022) and Volume II (July 2024) identified 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or then-territories between 1819 and 1969, at least 973 children's deaths, and at least 74 marked and unmarked burial sites at 65 schools. The report states that many Indian children suffered 'physical, sexual, and emotional abuse' at the schools and recommended a formal US apology.

title: Boy Scouts of America — 82,000+ abuse claims and bankruptcy settlement
who: Boy Scouts of America (now Scouting America) and local councils
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
cover_up: BSA kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers; 1,247 files from 1965–1985 were ordered released by the Oregon Supreme Court in June 2012 after a 2010 civil jury award of nearly $20 million.
what: BSA filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2020. By the November 2020 claims deadline more than 82,000 people had filed sexual abuse claims, which lawyers said was larger than all Catholic Church cases combined. A $2.46 billion settlement trust pays survivors between $3,500 and $2.7 million; the US Supreme Court declined to review the plan in January 2026. BSA's internal 'ineligible volunteer' files, which the Oregon Supreme Court ordered largely released in 2012, recorded suspected abusers over decades.

title: Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement
who: Los Angeles County Probation Department juvenile facilities; MacLaren Children's Center (closed 2003); county foster care
what: On 29 April 2025 the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a $4 billion settlement of more than 6,800 claims of sexual abuse, mostly in Probation Department juvenile facilities and at the MacLaren Children's Center in El Monte, plus foster care, dating back to the 1980s. It was the costliest such payout in county history.

title: New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester
who: State of New Hampshire Youth Development Center (juvenile detention)
what: More than 1,100 former residents of New Hampshire's state youth detention centre have sued over physical, sexual and emotional abuse spanning six decades, and 11 former state workers have been arrested. In the first trial, on 3 May 2024, a jury found the state negligent and awarded David Meehan, who went to police in 2017, $38 million. The state argued it was not liable for 'rogue' employees. A state settlement fund had paid $102 million on 206 claims by October 2024, with 448 more pending.

title: US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018
who: State and locally run juvenile detention and correctional facilities
what: The Bureau of Justice Statistics surveyed 6,049 youth in 327 juvenile facilities between March and December 2018. 7.1% reported sexual victimisation in the previous 12 months, and 5.8% reported sexual misconduct by staff (down from 7.7% in 2012). Youth-on-youth forced or coerced victimisation was reported by 1.9%.

title: Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'
who: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services; Health and Human Services Commission
cover_up: Judge Jack held Texas in contempt three times (2019, 2020, April 2024) for failing to investigate abuse complaints and protect children; in 2019 she said she could no longer find the department credible.
what: In a class action filed in 2011 on behalf of children in long-term state care, US District Judge Janis Graham Jack ruled in December 2015 that Texas violated foster children's constitutional rights by placing them in a system where 'rape and over-medication were the norm'. She later ordered 24-hour awake supervision and flagging of children who were victims or perpetrators of sexual violence. In April 2024 she found the state in contempt for a third time and fined it $100,000 a day over failures to investigate abuse reports.

title: 'Troubled teen' residential programmes — GAO 2007 investigation
who: Private residential treatment programmes, boot camps and wilderness programmes for youth
what: In testimony to Congress on 10 October 2007 (GAO-08-146T), the Government Accountability Office reported it had found thousands of allegations of abuse, some involving death, at residential treatment programmes for troubled youth, reviewing closed cases back to 1990. GAO did not verify each allegation.

title: Youth residential treatment facilities — US Senate Finance Committee 2024
who: Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health, Vivant Behavioral Healthcare (incl. former Sequel facilities); funded by Medicaid and child welfare agencies
what: A two-year Senate Finance Committee investigation released on 12 June 2024 found that 'horrific instances of sexual abuse persist unremediated' inside residential treatment facilities for children run by four large companies, along with physical abuse, overuse of restraints and overmedication. Facilities often receive more than $1,200 per child per day from Medicaid; states including Oregon sent foster children to out-of-state facilities.

title: Illinois state youth detention centres and Cook County JTDC — mass abuse lawsuits
who: Illinois Department of Juvenile Justice (nine state youth detention centres, five since closed); Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center
what: Between May and September 2024, 667 former detainees sued alleging sexual abuse by staff at Illinois state youth detention centres and the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center; three suits filed on 23 September 2024 alone covered 272 plaintiffs and abuse from 1996 to 2021. The lawsuits name repeat alleged abusers, including a chaplain at St. Charles, and say at least one accused employee still worked for the state. These are allegations not yet tested in court.

title: Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario)
who: Government of Ontario provincial training schools (juvenile reformatories)
what: In the class action Brown v. Ontario, the province agreed to a settlement of up to CAD 60 million, signed 21 January 2026 and approved by the Ontario Superior Court on 21 May 2026, for former residents of 13 provincial training schools between 1953 and 1984. It covers physical and sexual assault and solitary confinement. Ontario denies liability and the court did not decide the merits.

title: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
