cover_up: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').
what: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.

title: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
cover_up: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.
what: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.

title: Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry
who: Commonwealth, state and territory governments; church and state institutions, foster and adoptive families
cover_up: The report documented officials misrepresenting capable parents as unfit and telling some parents their children had died when they had not.
what: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 'Bringing Them Home' report on the forced removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children was released on 26 May 1997 with 54 recommendations. Survivors described abuse, including sexual abuse, in institutions and foster care. Recommendation five, a national apology, was refused by the Howard government and delivered by Prime Minister Kevin Rudd in 2008; the recommended national compensation scheme was refused by successive governments. The report recorded rates of sexual assault among its witnesses (record cites 17% of women and 7.7% of men among 502 witnesses; not re-checked from the report itself).

title: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
what: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.

title: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
what: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.

title: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
cover_up: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.
what: The Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory was set up in July 2016 after ABC Four Corners broadcast footage of boys at Don Dale being tear-gassed, hooded with spit hoods and shackled. Its final report, released on 17 November 2017 by commissioners Margaret White and Mick Gooda, found children had been subjected to 'regular, repeated and distressing mistreatment in detention' and that the law was often not followed, and recommended closing Don Dale, raising the age of criminal responsibility to 12 and not detaining children under 14.

title: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
cover_up: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.
what: Child-protection consultant Ian Elliott's 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published by Scouting Ireland on 14 May 2020, found a cover-up and failure to report abuse in the former Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and Scout Association of Ireland. It described 'a culture driven by self-interest', said 'cronyism thrived', and found that people suspected or known to be sex offenders gained positions of power and became 'largely impregnable'; records had been lost or destroyed, so the full extent could not be determined. An earlier audit reported to the Oireachtas in November 2018 had found evidence of 108 alleged victims and 71 alleged abusers, with numbers expected to rise considerably.

title: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cover_up: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.
what: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.

title: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cover_up: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.
what: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.

title: Lumos — 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights'
who: Mostly privately run, foreign-funded orphanages in Haiti; donors 92% from the US and 90% faith-based
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
what: Lumos researched Haiti's orphanages from October 2016 to February 2017, including a 2016 evaluation of 140 children in four orphanages with the government agency IBESR, and published its report in June 2017. It found at least US$70 million a year going to about a third of orphanages, with total funding estimated above $100 million a year; only 15% of orphanages were registered and at least 140 had conditions putting children at severe risk. It documented violence and severe neglect and, in a few cases, sexual abuse, trafficking and avoidable deaths, and evidence of orphanages recruiting children away from families — an 'orphanage business' it describes as increasingly recognised as trafficking.

title: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
cover_up: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.
what: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.

title: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cover_up: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.
what: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.

title: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
cover_up: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.
what: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.

title: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cover_up: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
what: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales

title: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cover_up: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.
what: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).

title: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cover_up: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.
what: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.

title: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
what: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.

title: Élan School, Poland, Maine — troubled-teen programme
who: Élan School (private behaviour-modification boarding school; NATSAP member)
cover_up: In the late 1970s staff refused a sheriff's lieutenant entry past the lobby after rumours of abuse.
what: Élan operated from 1970 until 1 April 2011, when it closed after decades of abuse reports from former students. Illinois officials removed eleven children in 1975 alleging mistreatment, and in 2007 New York education officials, who paid tuition for special-education students, alleged students were made to restrain peers and were sleep-deprived. The New Yorker (2000) and Time (2011) described 'the ring', in which students were made to fight one another. Maine State Police reopened the 1982 death of a 15-year-old student in 2016 but filed no charges. The record of sexual abuse rests on former students' accounts; no official sexual-abuse finding was located.

title: Provo Canyon School, Utah — licences revoked 2026
who: Provo Canyon School, owned by Universal Health Services (2000–2026)
what: Provo Canyon School opened in 1971 and has faced abuse allegations for more than 50 years; former students including Paris Hilton (who attended in the 1990s under different ownership) have publicly described abuse. In 2026, after a 13-year-old boy was seriously injured in a fight and staff did not call 911 or seek immediate care, Utah's Department of Health and Human Services revoked the licence of the school's Springville campus and, on 17 July 2026, of its original Provo campus, citing failure to protect children from harm and abuse, 'cruel and unnecessary' pain-compliance techniques, prolonged restraints and humiliating discipline. Owner Universal Health Services (since 2000) said it disagreed and was reviewing appeal options. No official sexual-abuse finding was located; the licence revocations concerned abuse, mistreatment and safety.

title: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
what: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.

title: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
what: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).

title: Scouts Canada — KPMG review of unreported abuse
who: Scouts Canada
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
cover_up: A 2011 CBC investigation found Scouts Canada had signed confidentiality agreements with more than a dozen abuse victims; KPMG found abusers had in some cases been 'removed discreetly' and records were inconsistent and poorly kept.
what: After a CBC investigation in autumn 2011 found confidentiality agreements that kept victims from speaking, Scouts Canada apologised and asked KPMG to audit 64 years of records. The review, released in 2012, examined 468 files and found the organisation failed at least 65 times to report sexual misconduct allegations to authorities, 13 of them after 1992 when reporting became mandatory. Scouts Canada then gave police all records it could find. In 1979 the Boy Scouts of America had sent a known abuser back to Canada without warning Scouts Canada; he was convicted in Victoria, BC in 1996 of assaulting four boys.

title: The Scout Association (UK) — abuse claims and payouts
who: The Scout Association (UK)
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
what: A BBC File on 4 investigation in June 2023 found, from data from eight specialist law firms, that at least 260 child sexual abuse claims had been taken on against the Scouts in the previous decade and more than £6m paid out across 166 settled cases. The Scouts said 96% of claims highlighted by a survivors' campaign related to offences before 2013 and that the payouts broadly matched what it knew. In 2014 the BBC had reported more than 50 historical claims and £897,000 in damages; an MP called for an inquiry into failures to pass abuse records to police.

title: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinder (VCP) — independent study of sexualised violence
who: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (VCP), Protestant scouting federation
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
cover_up: The study found 'old cases' from the 1980s and 1990s were long ignored for lack of any idea of reappraisal (Aufarbeitung).
what: A study by the Munich Institut für Praxisforschung und Projektberatung (IPP) and the Dissens Institute, presented in Kassel on 27 January 2026, found at least 344 people had suffered sexualised violence within the VCP since 1973. It drew on 79 interviews and about 1,300 pages of files on 100 cases. About 60% of victims were girls, two-thirds were aged 13–17 when it began, nearly half the acts occurred after 2000, and more than half on camps or trips. Perpetrators came mostly from within the organisation, often adult group leaders.

title: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
what: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.

title: Moldova — children leaving residential institutions targeted by traffickers
who: Moldovan state residential institutions and boarding schools (Ministry of Education, Health, Labour)
what: Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children in the mid-2000s; children left them at 15–16 with no support beyond about US$70 and no follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children and that 'they often become easy prey for traffickers'. The US State Department's March 2007 human rights report said women and children were trafficked for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel, the UAE and other countries, and that 12% of trafficking victims assisted by IOM were minors.

title: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
what: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.

title: Haiti — orphanage assessment identifies 3,019 potential trafficking victims
who: Private orphanages in Haiti; Institut du Bien-Être Social et de Recherches (IBESR)
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. IBESR closed eight non-compliant orphanages in the reporting period and expanded foster care to 121 accredited families to reduce children's vulnerability to trafficking.

title: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
cover_up: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.
what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.

title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

title: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cover_up: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.
what: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.

title: Dow Family Children's Home, Kenya — US conviction of founder
who: Dow Family Children's Home, founded 2008 by US missionary Gregory Dow
what: Gregory Dow, from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, opened an orphanage in Kenya in 2008 and sexually abused four girls aged 11 to 13 when the abuse began, between October 2013 and September 2017. He fled to the US after Kenyan authorities issued an arrest warrant; the home closed in September 2017. He was arrested in July 2019 and in June 2020 pleaded guilty in federal court in Philadelphia to four counts of illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place.

title: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
cover_up: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.
what: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.

title: Lechaina Children's Care Centre, Greece — caged beds and sedation
who: State Children Care Center of Lechaina (children with disabilities)
what: In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman's Office published a report on the state care centre at Lechaina finding too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds and the use of wooden cage beds because of staff shortages; most children received no education. In 2012 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern about the centre. A BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. This is a record of institutional abuse and neglect; no sexual-abuse finding was located.

title: Serbia — 'Torment not Treatment' investigation of institutions for children and adults with disabilities
who: Serbian state institutions for people with mental disabilities
cover_up: In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave; Serbian officials called the allegations 'dark propaganda'.
what: Mental Disability Rights International's four-year investigation, released on 14 November 2007, covered conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities in Serbian institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy conditions, contagious disease and no oversight, treatment it said was 'tantamount to torture'. It warned of a danger of sexual exploitation: at Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards and staff said they made no effort to determine whether sex was consensual.

title: Mogilino home for children with disabilities, Bulgaria
who: Bulgarian state institution for children with physical and mental disabilities
what: The BBC film 'Bulgaria's Abandoned Children' (2007, Kate Blewett) documented neglect of disabled children at the Mogilino state home. On 22 February 2008 Bulgaria's Labour and Social Policy Minister repeated a promise to close Mogilino and six similar homes, and by June 2008 children were being moved, with UNICEF working towards closure. Bulgaria has been criticised for having one of the highest numbers of children in state institutions in the EU. No sexual-abuse finding was located; this is a neglect record.

title: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes
who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
what: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. The review followed a case in Soacha in which a man was jailed on charges of sexually abusing two girls aged 7 and 8 who were in ICBF custody in a foster home; he did not accept the charges.

title: Russia — 'Abandoned by the State': violence and neglect in orphanages for children with disabilities
who: Russian state orphanages for children with disabilities
cover_up: Children had few if any meaningful ways to seek help or report abuse; health workers pressured parents to give up disabled children.
what: Human Rights Watch's report of 15 September 2014, based on more than 200 interviews and visits to 10 state orphanages, found that many children with disabilities suffered serious abuse and neglect by staff, including beatings, sedative injections and being sent to psychiatric hospitals as punishment. Children deemed most severely disabled were confined to cribs in 'lying-down rooms', often tied to furniture. The report did not centre on sexual abuse; it is recorded here as institutional abuse and removal of children from families.

title: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cover_up: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.
what: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.

title: Anuradhapura children's home — probation officials arrested
who: North Central Provincial Department of Probation and Child Care Services
what: After a media report on 8 January 2021 of illegal activity at a children's home near Anuradhapura and a complaint by the National Child Protection Authority on 16 January 2021, police arrested a former provincial Commissioner and a Senior Probation Officer of the Department of Probation and Child Care Services. They were accused over the treatment of a 17-year-old girl held at a counselling centre on court orders who was made to work as a cook in a children's home. They were granted bail by the Anuradhapura Magistrate's Court and the Attorney General's advice was sought on further action.

title: Hogar del Huérfano, Rosario — two former carers convicted
who: Hogar del Huérfano (children's home), Rosario
what: Two former carers (celadores) at Rosario's Hogar del Huérfano were found to have repeatedly sexually abused a boy aged nine housed there between January 2009 and May 2011. The report came from the boy's substitute family and was taken to court by the Santa Fe province children's department. They were sentenced to 15 years in October 2016, the verdict was annulled on technical grounds in 2017, and on 22 August 2020 they were again sentenced to 15 years; they remained free pending a final ruling.

title: Panama — legislative subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters
who: Private and NGO shelters (albergues) under the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf)
cover_up: The Ombudsman found 70% of 44 shelters inspected lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.
what: A National Assembly subcommission report in early February 2021 found cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. By March 2021 the Public Ministry had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected.

title: Project Pierre Toussaint, Cap-Haïtien — founder convicted in US
who: Project Pierre Toussaint residential school and programme for street boys, founded by Douglas Perlitz; funded by Catholic donors in Fairfield and Westchester counties (Fairfield University, Order of Malta later involved in handover)
what: Douglas Perlitz ran an intake centre, residential school and group homes for street boys in Cap-Haïtien. Students went public with abuse accounts in 2007 and the programme shut in summer 2009 when funding ended. In August 2010 he pleaded guilty in federal court in Connecticut to travelling from New York to Haiti to have sex with a minor, and on 21 December 2010 US District Judge Janet Bond Arterton sentenced him to 19 years and seven months for the systematic and prolonged abuse of at least 16 boys in his care.

title: Japan — Yomiuri survey of sexual misconduct by staff in children's homes
who: Children's homes (児童養護施設) in Japan
what: A Yomiuri Shimbun survey published in December 2021 found that in the five years to fiscal 2020 at least 47 staff at children's homes across Japan were confirmed to have committed indecent acts against children in their care, and that 69 children were victims. Only a summary of the survey was accessible; the full article was withdrawn by the provider.

title: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
cover_up: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.
what: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.

title: Brazil — children placed from institutional care for adoption raped and tortured by guardian
who: Prospective adoptive guardian with provisional custody during the pre-adoption placement period; children came from institutional care (acolhimento)
what: On 24 April 2023 a court in Santo Antônio das Missões, at the request of the Rio Grande do Sul Public Ministry, sentenced a man to 46 years and 6 months for rape of a vulnerable person and torture, plus 8 months for mistreatment. During 2020 he repeatedly raped and tortured two siblings aged 7 and 8 who had left institutional care and were in his provisional custody for an adoption trial period. The judge noted the children had left institutional care hoping for an adoptive home.

title: Uganda — over 500 unlicensed children's homes outside state oversight
who: Uganda Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development; unlicensed children's homes, many foreign-funded
network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
what: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed (holding 9,486 children) and that more than 500 unlicensed institutions operate without oversight, exposing children to neglect, exploitation and abuse. The ministry's principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans, and that some are survivors of trafficking or sexual abuse. The government has closed unregistered homes, including Hope Center Uganda (American board) after a raid that found children in poor conditions.

title: Netherlands — Scout leader convicted of abusing girls and producing abuse material
who: Local Scouting group (Scouting Nederland member group not named by the court)
network: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
what: In September 2019 the Overijssel District Court sentenced a 20-year-old man from Friesland to two years in prison and TBS (compulsory psychiatric treatment) for sexually abusing four girls, two of whom he led in Scouting, secretly photographing two girls including in a shower at a Scout campsite, and producing and distributing abuse material online. He was ordered to pay more than €50,000 in damages.

title: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
cover_up: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.
what: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.

title: Apna Ghar shelter, Rohtak — CBI court convictions
who: Apna Ghar, a government-funded shelter run by Jaswanti Devi and relatives
what: The case began in 2012 when three girls escaped from the government-funded Apna Ghar shelter and told police residents were physically and sexually abused and used as bonded labour. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights raided it in May 2012; Haryana sealed it in June 2012 and the CBI charge-sheeted ten people in August 2012. On 18 April 2018 a special CBI court in Panchkula convicted nine, including of rape, abortion without consent, bonded labour and offences under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and Juvenile Justice Act; on 27 April 2018 Jaswanti Devi, her son-in-law and a driver were sentenced to life. A former child development project officer who oversaw the shelter was acquitted.

title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

title: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.

title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.

title: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
network: Operation Sangaris (French army, CAR)
cover_up: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.
what: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.

title: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

title: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.
what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.

title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.
what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.

title: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.

title: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study)
who: UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) soldiers
network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
what: The UN study 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children' led by Graça Machel (August 1996) found that after the 1992 peace treaty, ONUMOZ soldiers recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. It also found that in 6 of 12 country studies on sexual exploitation of children in armed conflict, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was associated with a rapid rise in child prostitution.

title: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
cover_up: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.
what: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.

title: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
what: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
network: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM)
what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

title: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cover_up: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).
what: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
